text: uniqueness and Lipschitz stability for recovering piecewise constant diffusion coefficient in one-dimensional parabolic equation from interior point measurements For a Lipschitz domain D, given functions a and b in class A1, and a positive bounded function f, the L2 norm of the difference between a and b is bounded by a constant times the H01 norm of the difference between their corresponding solutions raised to the power one-sixth. The constant depends on the domain, dimension, ellipticity parameters, and the lower bound of f. The inequality also involves a constant C0 from a prior definition. This result provides a stability estimate for the inverse problem of recovering coefficients from solutions. There exists exactly one real constant such that a particular equation has a solution. This solution is a Lipschitz continuous function defined on the closure of a domain. The constant is uniquely determined. The solution exists for that specific constant. The problem describes a diffusion equation with a positive, integrable coefficient function. It states that the initial value problem has at most one solution. This uniqueness holds under the condition that the solution is square integrable over space. Under certain smoothness and support conditions on the initial data, and with given functions satisfying continuity and non-vanishing properties, the inverse problem has a unique solution. The coefficient function is continuous on the time interval. The assumptions ensure the associated equation is uniformly parabolic.

text: neural network approximation rates for Lipschitz inverse maps of finite-dimensional parameters from time series observations sample complexity A Lipschitz map's inverse can be approximated by a neural network when the domain is compact and network weights are bounded. The network's depth, width, and weight bound are chosen based on the domain dimension and Lipschitz constant. The learning error is bounded by an expression involving the Lipschitz constant, domain radius, and network parameters. This bound also depends on the number of training samples and includes absolute constants. For any Lipschitz function on a domain, there exists a neural network with a specific depth and bounded parameters that approximates the function. The depth of the network grows logarithmically with the number of parameters and the input dimension. The approximation error is bounded by a constant times the inverse of the number of parameters raised to the power of one over the dimension. This holds for any sufficiently small positive error tolerance. If the inverse map from observations to the original matrix is Lipschitz continuous, then a Johnson-Lindenstrauss embedding exists for the set of possible observations with a dimension depending on the Lipschitz constant and other parameters. For this embedding dimension, there is a ReLU neural network architecture that can approximate the inverse map to within a given error over any bounded subset of observations. The network's size is bounded in terms of the number of edges, nodes, and layers. These bounds depend on the Lipschitz constant, the error tolerance, and the maximum infinity norm of the embedded observations. For functions in the Lipschitz class, the uniform norm of the difference between the function and its neural network approximation is bounded by a constant times the Lipschitz norm divided by the number of parameters. The approximation error decreases as the number of parameters increases. The bound is proportional to the inverse of the parameter count. This result holds for neural networks with a specified architecture.

title: Proposition 10 — Neural Network Approximation of Continuous Functions in High Dimensions with Applications to Inverse Problems
text: If the inverse map from observations to the original matrix is Lipschitz continuous, then a Johnson-Lindenstrauss embedding exists for the set of possible observations with a dimension depending on the Lipschitz constant and other parameters. For this embedding dimension, there is a ReLU neural network architecture that can approximate the inverse map to within a given error over any bounded subset of observations. The network's size is bounded in terms of the number of edges, nodes, and layers. These bounds depend on the Lipschitz constant, the error tolerance, and the maximum infinity norm of the embedded observations. Suppose the mask is chosen so that the inverse map $F^{-1}: \boldsymbol{Y} =P_{\Omega }(\boldsymbol{X} ) \rightarrow \boldsymbol{X} $ is Lipschitz continuous with Lipschitz constant $L$. Then, for any $\rho \in (0,\tfrac {1}{2})$, there exists a $\rho $-JL embedding $A : \mathbb{R} ^{m \times n} \to \mathbb{R} ^d$ of the set of possible observations $$\mathcal {Y} = \{P_{\Omega }(\boldsymbol{X} ): \boldsymbol{X} \in M^{m,n}_r \cap \mathcal {C}\},$$ into $\mathbb{R} ^d$ provided that $$d \gtrsim \rho ^{-2}r(m+n)\log \dfrac {L\sqrt {mn}}{\rho }.$$ For such choice of $d$, we have that for any bounded subset $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathcal {Y}$, there exists a ReLU neural network architecture with at most $$(mn+C_1)\left (2\ceil {\dfrac {LM\sqrt {d}}{(1-\rho )\epsilon }}+1\right )^d + mnd \ \text {edges},$$ $$C_2\left (2\ceil {\dfrac {LM\sqrt {d}}{(1-\rho )\epsilon }}+1\right )^d + 2mn \ \text {nodes},$$ $$\text {and} \ \left \lceil \log _2(d+1) \right \rceil + 3 \ \text {layers}$$ which can $\epsilon $-approximate the inverse map $F^{-1}$ over the set $\mathcal{S} $. Here $M = \max _{\boldsymbol{Y} \in \mathcal{S} }\|\text {vec}(A(\boldsymbol{Y} ))\|_{\infty }$

text: Lipschitz stability for identification of piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in parabolic equation from interior or boundary point measurements The inverse Robin problem for parabolic equations is locally Lipschitz stable. If the solution is bounded below by a positive constant on the inner boundary over time, then the difference in solutions on the accessible boundary controls the difference in Robin coefficients. This holds for all coefficients in a neighborhood of a given coefficient. The stability constant depends on the lower bound and the neighborhood size. The theorem establishes a stability estimate for the difference between two conductivity functions in a domain. It bounds the L-infinity norm of their difference on an inner subdomain by a sum of boundary differences and solution differences raised to a fractional power. The constants depend on domain parameters, boundary data, and operator coefficients. Under analytic boundary and coefficient conditions, the estimate holds on the entire domain. The theorem applies to a bounded Lipschitz domain with certain coefficient functions. It assumes specific boundary conditions and right-hand side functionals. There exists a stability constant independent of the forcing terms. This constant bounds the solutions of the given equations. For a Lipschitz domain with given parameters, if the L2 norm difference of two weak solutions on a boundary part is bounded by epsilon, then the L-infinity norm difference of the corresponding coefficients on a specific inner boundary region is bounded by a function of epsilon. This function is the composition of eta with itself applied to epsilon. The result establishes a stability estimate for the coefficients based on the solutions' proximity.

text: uniqueness of diffusion coefficient recovery in one-dimensional heat equation from measurements at finitely many interior points over a time interval Given a time T greater than zero and a sequence of times converging to a value between zero and T, consider two initial conditions and two coefficients, each with support conditions. The theorem states that if the spatial derivatives of the corresponding solutions at the boundary point x equals one are equal at each time in the sequence, then the initial conditions and coefficients must be identical. This implies that boundary measurements at a discrete set of times can uniquely determine both the initial data and the coefficient function. The inverse problem of identifying the conductivity coefficient, heat source, and solution from a final temperature measurement in a heat equation has a unique solution. This holds under specific regularity conditions on the initial data and final measurement. The conductivity coefficient and heat source belong to a defined set with certain properties. The solution must also satisfy boundedness conditions on the gradient and Laplacian of its time derivative. The problem describes a diffusion equation with a positive, integrable coefficient function. It states that the initial value problem has at most one solution. This uniqueness holds under the condition that the solution is square integrable over space. The solution exists and is unique for all positive time when the diffusion coefficients are equal.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Smooth nonlinear map: noise-augmented MLP on standardized raw traces with log-k targets reaches rel_l2 <= 0.05
text: The inverse map from 4-sensor time traces to (k1..k4) is smooth and well-conditioned over the prior box. Sensor noise (sigma=0.001) is small relative to the trace signal. The remaining error is therefore approximation error, not irreducible noise. A torch MLP trained on log-k with Gaussian noise augmentation at the true sigma should reach val rel_l2 <= 0.05. That is a >6x reduction from the mean baseline (0.3307). Measurement-design view: the sensors at indices 5, 15, 25, 35 sit roughly in the middle of each of the four segments, if the segments are equal quarters of the 40-point grid. Each sensor's decay rate and arrival time is then dominated by its local k, with coupling through the interfaces, so the map should be locally injective. Conductivity enters multiplicatively (diffusion time scales ~1/k), which makes log-k the natural target scale. Augmenting with noise at the stated sigma matches the training distribution to the test noise model and acts as Tikhonov-like regularisation. This guards against the network fitting noise-free fine structure that it cannot see at test time. Train, val and test are generated by the same simulator and noise model (sigma=0.001 i.i.d.), so the noise-augmented training distribution matches test. Sensor index i maps to segment floor(i/10), so each segment has exactly one interior sensor; this is unverified. The explicit FD scheme is stable for k up to 2 (CFL), so traces are physical and not blown-up artefacts. 3000 samples are enough to cover a 4-D box densely for a smooth map; that is about 7 points per axis.

The explicit FD scheme is stable for k up to 2 (CFL), so traces are physical and not blown-up artefacts.

data.falsifiable_test: Compare val rel_l2 against the threshold of 0.05. Also report per-parameter error: if k1/k4 errors are more than 2x the k2/k3 errors, the boundary-segment information-deficit explanation is supported over model-capacity limits. Control: the same model with noise_aug=0. If augmentation does not help or hurts, noise is not the limiting factor.
data.if_fails: If val rel_l2 lands in 0.05-0.1 with errors concentrated on k1/k4, the limit is measurement information at the boundary segments rather than the learner. The next step would be a posterior-mean-style estimator that shrinks toward the prior. If errors are uniform across parameters, it is approximation or sample-size limited, and kernel methods or PCA-compressed inputs should be tried.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Competing explanation: traces lie on a low-dimensional manifold, so PCA-compressed kernel ridge matches or beats the MLP
text: The 4 sensor traces are smooth in time and driven by a 4-parameter family, so the observation manifold is about 4-dimensional and well captured by roughly 30 PCA components. Most of the remaining variance is noise. RBF kernel ridge on the PCA-whitened features with a log-k target will achieve val rel_l2 <= 0.05 and land within 20% of the best data-driven model. If instead the kernel model is more than 50% worse than the best data-driven model, the inverse map has strongly anisotropic structure that a single-bandwidth RBF cannot capture. Simulation fidelity and data-distribution view: heat-equation solutions are dominated by a few decaying eigenmodes. Time traces are therefore highly redundant, with high-index PCA components mostly noise. Projecting onto the leading components denoises the input and is a cheap form of spectral truncation. It also makes the isotropic RBF bandwidth heuristic meaningful. This arm is a cheap, low-variance control for the MLP hypothesis. It distinguishes 'smooth map, any good interpolant works' from 'needs learned feature extraction'. Parabolic smoothing makes the leading PCA components capture almost all of the signal variance; the noise is white and spread across all components. The kernel bandwidth heuristic (gamma_mult=1 on standardized features) is within an order of magnitude of optimal; the harness may tune it. O(n^2) memory with n=3000 is feasible.

assumptions: Parabolic smoothing makes the leading PCA components capture almost all of the signal variance; the noise is white and spread across all components.
The kernel bandwidth heuristic (gamma_mult=1 on standardized features) is within an order of magnitude of optimal; the harness may tune it.
O(n^2) memory with n=3000 is feasible.
data.falsifiable_test: Measure val rel_l2 and compare it with the best data-driven arm. Prediction: rel_l2 <= 0.05 and within 20% of the best data-driven model. Falsified if the kernel model is worse than 0.05, or more than 50% worse than the best data-driven arm. Secondary check: rerun with pca=10 versus 60. If the error is flat across these, the manifold dimension is low as claimed; if it improves strongly with more components, information sits in low-variance directions.
data.if_fails: Failure would show that the discriminative information lies in low-variance PCA directions, likely late-time or boundary-sensor tails, or that the map is too anisotropic for an isotropic kernel. That argues for learned features (MLP), no PCA, or per-sensor normalisation.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Multiplicative-scale learned inverse: log-conductivity targets with physical-noise augmentation
text: The inverse map from sensor time series to k is closer to smooth and homoscedastic when written in log k. Under the uniform prior, an MLP trained on log k with noise augmentation at the true sigma=0.001 will reach val rel_l2 < 0.05. The same MLP trained on raw k targets without augmentation will be measurably worse, with a val rel_l2 gap of at least 15%. The framing treats k as additive targets. Heat diffusion depends on k through time scales of order L^2/k, so sensor responses are naturally functions of log k. The local sensitivity |dU/dk| goes like 1/k, so absolute errors grow with k while relative errors stay roughly constant in log space. The rel_l2 metric is dominated by the large-k segments, which are exactly where raw-scale regression is least informed. Augmenting with the stated measurement noise trains the network on the true observation distribution rather than on a clean manifold, which regularises it against noise-amplifying directions. No forward model is available, so a learned direct inverse is the main admissible route. Each simulated training feature row already contains noise with sigma=0.001, so augmentation adds a second, comparable draw rather than mismatched noise. The harness's noise_scale is a multiplier on the stated noise std. The forward map is injective on [0.5,2]^4 from 4 interior sensors over 200 steps, at least practically for segments that are not shadowed. This is not proven here; the retrieved uniqueness results do not transfer (see citations). 3000 samples is enough to cover a 4-D box densely, at roughly 7 points per axis on a grid-equivalent scale.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Simulator-free physics inversion: learn an emulator of the forward map from training pairs, then solve a noise-weighted inverse problem per sample
text: Training data contains (theta, observation) pairs, so the missing forward model can be learned as a differentiable emulator f: log k -> standardized observations. For each val sample, start from an amortized inverse-net estimate and minimise a residual weighted by the emulator's own error variance, with a weak prior pull. This will reduce val rel_l2 by at least 10% relative to the inverse net alone. The reason is that the forward direction (4 -> ~800, smooth and well-posed) is easier to learn than the inverse direction (ill-posed), and refinement exploits all 800 residuals rather than a regression bottleneck. This challenges the assumption that no forward model means no physics-style inversion. In the forward problem, small parameter changes give stable, smooth observation changes, so a learned forward map can be more accurate than a learned inverse, which must also absorb noise and near-non-identifiability. Combining amortized inference (ML) with variational data assimilation (inverse-problems tradition) through a surrogate is a standard move in UQ, but it is absent from the library menu. Weighting by the emulator residual variance plus sigma^2 keeps the refinement from chasing emulator bias. The emulator's error in standardized observation space can be driven well below the inverse-induced error in observation space. Otherwise refinement only adds emulator bias. The emulator-residual weighted loss is locally well conditioned near the initializer. A 4-parameter problem with about 800 data points should satisfy this unless segments are shadowed. Features are the raw flattened sensor-time series, and the ordering is irrelevant to the code. Bounds are hard-coded to [0.5,2.0], matching the stated problem, to avoid relying on the context object's interface.

data.falsifiable_test: Report val rel_l2 for the inverse net alone (refine_steps=0) and for the refined estimate. The hypothesis is falsified if refinement does not improve val rel_l2 by >= 10% relative to refine_steps=0. It is also falsified if the emulator's held-out residual, in standardized units, is not smaller than the observation-space residual of the inverse net's predictions. Secondary check: the improvement should concentrate on samples where the inverse net's error is largest.
data.if_fails: If refinement hurts, the emulator's systematic bias exceeds the information gain. In that case the learned-forward route needs a higher-capacity or physics-structured emulator (e.g. a modal/exponential-decay basis), or should be used only as a likelihood for posterior reweighting rather than as a point-estimate optimiser. If the inverse-net baseline is already below 0.05, refinement is unnecessary and the gain should be measured instead in calibration of the outer segments.

author: researcher-ml
title: TheoremSearch: torch_mlp on log features with log-conductivity targets
text: torch_mlp on log features with log-conductivity targets An overparameterized two-layer MLP trained with gradient descent learns a target function composed of monomials. The sample complexity depends on the structure of the target function's components. It scales with the sum of weighted norms of the component parameters. The bound also includes a logarithmic term in the number of outputs and failure probability. The multilayer perceptron has a depth bounded by the logarithm of the input dimension plus four. The final layer's weights depend on the target function, while all earlier layers depend only on the input dimension and have zero biases. Weights in intermediate layers take values of zero or plus or minus one half. The initial and final weight matrices are bounded in magnitude by one and the maximum function value, respectively, and bias terms are bounded by the sample size. Under certain assumptions, the expected regret of EMLP is bounded by a constant times d log T. The constant depends only on F(omega) and is independent of the distribution D. The bound holds for strictly log-concave, convex, and bounded settings with i.i.d. features. A functional network with M nonzero parameters approximates a target functional over a compact function space. The approximation error decays at a rate involving logarithms of M. The depth of the network grows at most like the square of log M divided by log log M. The result holds under specific smoothness conditions on the functional and input space.

author: literature
title: Theorem 3 (Overall regret) — Logarithmic Regret in Feature-based Dynamic Pricing
text: Under certain assumptions, the expected regret of EMLP is bounded by a constant times d log T. The constant depends only on F(omega) and is independent of the distribution D. The bound holds for strictly log-concave, convex, and bounded settings with i.i.d. features. With Assumptions \ref {assumption_strictly_log_concave}, \ref {assumption_convex_feature_and_parameter_set}, \ref {assumption_bounded_x_set} and \ref {random_iid_xt}, the expected regret of EMLP can be bounded by: \begin {equation} \mathbb {E}[Reg_{\text {EMLP}}]\leq 2C_{s}{d}{\log {T}}, \end {equation} where $C_{s}$ is a constant that depends only on $F(\omega )$ and is independent to $\mathbb {D}$.

author: literature
title: Theorem 4 — Nonlinear functional regression by functional deep neural network with kernel embedding
text: A functional network with M nonzero parameters approximates a target functional over a compact function space. The approximation error decays at a rate involving logarithms of M. The depth of the network grows at most like the square of log M divided by log log M. The result holds under specific smoothness conditions on the functional and input space. Let $\alpha ,d,M \in \mathbb N $, $\Omega =[0,1]^d$. Assume that the input function space $\mathcal {F}$ is a compact subset of the unit ball of the mixed smooth Sobolev space $H_{mix}^\alpha (\Omega )$, and the modulus of continuity of the target functional $F: \mathcal {F} \to \mathbb R $ adheres to the condition (\ref {functionalsmoothness}) with $\lambda \in (0,1]$. By selecting the embedding kernel $K$ as defined in \eqref {embeddingkernelm}, the projection kernel $K_0$ as $K_\alpha $, and \begin {equation} \label {hyper3} d_1 = C_4 \frac {\log M}{\log \log M}, \end {equation} there exists a functional network $F_{NN}$ that follows the architecture specified in Definition \ref {deffunctionalNN}, with $M$ nonzero parameters and the depth \begin {equation} J \leq C_5 \left ( \frac {\log M}{\log \log M}\right )^2, \end {equation} such that \begin {equation} \sup _{f\in \mathcal {F}} |F(f)-F_{NN}(f)| \leq C_6 (\log M)^{-\alpha \lambda } (\log \log M)^{(d-2)\alpha \lambda }, \end {equation} where $C_4, C_5,C_6$ are positive constants.

title: TheoremSearch: Training-set shape and the time sampling of features
text: Training-set shape and the time sampling of features Under certain conditions on the data distribution and activation functions, there exist constants depending on a parameter delta. The theorem assumes bounded and smooth activation functions with Lipschitz derivatives, and a sufficiently large sample size relative to dimension. It defines a specific time interval based on these parameters. Within this interval, the maximum difference between two sets of parameters is bounded by a term that decays with sample size. The training error for the random feature model decays exponentially with time. The deviation between the trained and linearized model functions is bounded. This holds with high probability when the number of features is sufficiently large relative to the dataset size and minimum eigenvalue. The bounds depend on the number of features, time, and the minimum eigenvalue of the kernel matrix. The theorem provides a lower bound on the difference between a trained discriminator and an optimal discriminator over time. This bound holds with high probability when sampling from a given distribution. The bound depends on the dimension, sample size, and time elapsed during training. It combines terms related to the curse of dimensionality and statistical estimation error. The theorem considers a training curve reaching a specific parameter value. It assumes the curve remains in a majority-advancing set after that point. For any small positive epsilon, the time required to reduce the loss difference by a factor of epsilon is considered. This time difference grows without bound as epsilon approaches zero.

title: TheoremSearch: Log-linearisation of diffusive decay
text: Log-linearisation of diffusive decay If solutions to a linear equation decay exponentially near the origin, then solutions to the corresponding linearized equation also decay exponentially. title: TheoremSearch: Per-parameter val error and its correlation with k magnitude
text: Per-parameter val error and its correlation with k magnitude The minimum value over a set K has an error bound between its true value and an approximation using a parameter k. This bound applies when k is at least the dimension d and all components of the parameter vector are equal to k. The upper bound on the error is proportional to the sum of Lipschitz constants divided by k. It also involves a binomial coefficient and a polynomial term in n raised to the dimension d. For a specific index k and parameter choices, the error term epsilon sub t is bounded with high probability. The error is defined as the difference between the objective value at the estimate and the minimum objective value over all matrices. This bound is expressed in terms of the parameters K, m, k, d, eta, and epsilon sub t. The bound scales as a constant times K cubed times the square root of m times k times d times log d, divided by the product of eta and epsilon sub t. The inequality holds for all k where a certain error term is at most one over four times L. The upper bound is expressed as a product of constants, squared L, and two error terms. This product multiplies the expected squared distance from the current parameter to the optimal parameter. It also includes a term involving the norm of the optimal parameter plus one, all squared. The error term from the referenced theorem is minimized when k equals one. At this value, the error term equals two times p.

title: TheoremSearch: Per-feature min/median of training observations, by sensor and time
text: Per-feature min/median of training observations, by sensor and time The aggregate explanation equals the feature-wise sample median when using the L1 distance metric and setting parameter p to 1. A number m is a median of a random variable X with finite expected absolute value if and only if the expected absolute deviation from m equals the minimum possible expected absolute deviation over all real numbers. This means that m minimizes the function that maps a real number a to the expected value of the absolute difference between X and a. The condition requires that the expectation of |X - m| is as small as it can be for any choice of a. The function f evaluated at any input vector equals the median of three values: f evaluated with the k-th coordinate set to zero, the function Phi_k evaluated at the k-th coordinate, and f evaluated with the k-th coordinate set to one. This holds for every coordinate k and every input vector. The median is the same whether using Phi_k^- or Phi_k^+ for the middle term. The result requires that f satisfies two specific conditions. The clone generated by the median function of three elements is minimal.

text: identifiability of piecewise constant conductivity from interior point measurements heat equation 1-D The inverse problem of identifying the conductivity coefficient, heat source, and solution from a final temperature measurement in a heat equation has a unique solution. This holds under specific regularity conditions on the initial data and final measurement. The conductivity coefficient and heat source belong to a defined set with certain properties. The solution must also satisfy boundedness conditions on the gradient and Laplacian of its time derivative. The theorem considers a bounded domain with two nested inclusions and defines piecewise constant conductivities. It examines solutions to a modified conductivity equation with a given boundary flux. If the boundary values of the solutions for the two inclusions coincide, then the solutions are identical throughout the domain. This implies the two inclusions must be the same set. The voltage-to-heat flow map uniquely determines the conductivity. The Neumann kernel uniquely determines the conductivity on a set where it is constant, given that the potential is positive on a subset of positive measure. This holds under the hypotheses of the referenced theorem. The kernel is known for all points on a specified boundary portion.

The log transform maps their N(0, 1e-3) noise onto large, heavy-tailed feature values, which lowers the effective SNR. So this arm will be WORSE than the raw-feature log-y MLP (P-005/P-NEW), mainly on k1 and k4, while k2/k3 errors stay comparable. Diffusive time scales scale with 1/k, which is why log targets are well motivated. Log features linearise exponential decay only where the signal is far above the noise. Near Dirichlet boundaries and at early times, the signal is comparable to sigma. A per-parameter contrast tells us whether the feature transform or the learner limits accuracy. author: researcher-experimental
title: Smooth nonlinear map: noise-augmented MLP on standardized raw traces with log-k targets reaches rel_l2 <= 0.05
text: The inverse map from 4-sensor time traces to (k1..k4) is smooth and well-conditioned over the prior box. Sensor noise (sigma=0.001) is small relative to the trace signal. The remaining error is therefore approximation error, not irreducible noise. A torch MLP trained on log-k with Gaussian noise augmentation at the true sigma should reach val rel_l2 <= 0.05. That is a >6x reduction from the mean baseline (0.3307). Measurement-design view: the sensors at indices 5, 15, 25, 35 sit roughly in the middle of each of the four segments, if the segments are equal quarters of the 40-point grid. Each sensor's decay rate and arrival time is then dominated by its local k, with coupling through the interfaces, so the map should be locally injective. Conductivity enters multiplicatively (diffusion time scales ~1/k), which makes log-k the natural target scale. Augmenting with noise at the stated sigma matches the training distribution to the test noise model and acts as Tikhonov-like regularisation. This guards against the network fitting noise-free fine structure that it cannot see at test time. Train, val and test are generated by the same simulator and noise model (sigma=0.001 i.i.d.), so the noise-augmented training distribution matches test. Sensor index i maps to segment floor(i/10), so each segment has exactly one interior sensor; this is unverified. The explicit FD scheme is stable for k up to 2 (CFL), so traces are physical and not blown-up artefacts. 3000 samples are enough to cover a 4-D box densely for a smooth map; that is about 7 points per axis. Sensor-segment mapping: verify whether segments are equal quarters (indices 0-9, 10-19, ...). If they are, sensors 5/15/25/35 sit mid-segment.

If errors are uniform across parameters, it is approximation or sample-size limited, and kernel methods or PCA-compressed inputs should be tried.

author: researcher-experimental
title: Competing explanation: traces lie on a low-dimensional manifold, so PCA-compressed kernel ridge matches or beats the MLP
text: The 4 sensor traces are smooth in time and driven by a 4-parameter family, so the observation manifold is about 4-dimensional and well captured by roughly 30 PCA components. Most of the remaining variance is noise. RBF kernel ridge on the PCA-whitened features with a log-k target will achieve val rel_l2 <= 0.05 and land within 20% of the best data-driven model. If instead the kernel model is more than 50% worse than the best data-driven model, the inverse map has strongly anisotropic structure that a single-bandwidth RBF cannot capture. Simulation fidelity and data-distribution view: heat-equation solutions are dominated by a few decaying eigenmodes. Time traces are therefore highly redundant, with high-index PCA components mostly noise. Projecting onto the leading components denoises the input and is a cheap form of spectral truncation. It also makes the isotropic RBF bandwidth heuristic meaningful. This arm is a cheap, low-variance control for the MLP hypothesis. It distinguishes 'smooth map, any good interpolant works' from 'needs learned feature extraction'. Parabolic smoothing makes the leading PCA components capture almost all of the signal variance; the noise is white and spread across all components. The kernel bandwidth heuristic (gamma_mult=1 on standardized features) is within an order of magnitude of optimal; the harness may tune it. O(n^2) memory with n=3000 is feasible. Run PCA on raw unscaled features, or scale each channel by sigma, then whiten the retained components.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: Learned-forward-model inversion: emulator-weighted batched Levenberg-Marquardt refinement of an amortized inverse, with holdout self-gating
text: A 2-member MLP emulator log k -> observations, trained on the training pairs, has raw-unit holdout RMSE within a small multiple (<5x) of sigma=0.001. Levenberg-Marquardt refinement of the inverse-net estimate under the emulator likelihood then reduces val rel_l2 by at least 10% relative to the inverse net alone. If emulator RMSE >> sigma, the gate will disable refinement and the method reverts to the inverse net. This is itself a falsification of the 'forward easier than inverse' claim at this data size. No forward model does not mean no likelihood. The pairs define one empirically. The forward direction (4 -> D, smooth parabolic solution map) is a low-input-dimension regression, while the inverse direction must also absorb noise and near-non-identifiability. Per-sample Gauss-Newton uses all D residuals instead of a regression bottleneck. This is variational data assimilation through a learned surrogate, structurally distinct from the other 7 data-driven arms. Emulator raw-unit error can be made comparable to sigma with 2550 training pairs. This is the crux and is measured internally. The emulator-weighted LM problem is well conditioned near the initializer for most samples. Features are flattened sensor time series and their ordering is irrelevant. Bounds are hard-coded to [0.5, 2.0] per the stated problem.

The emulator-weighted LM problem is well conditioned near the initializer for most samples.
Features are flattened sensor time series and their ordering is irrelevant.
Bounds are hard-coded to [0.5, 2.0] per the stated problem.
data.falsifiable_test: Run with refine_iters=20 and refine_iters=0 (inverse net alone, same seeds and split). Falsified if the refined val rel_l2 is not at least 10% below the refine_iters=0 val rel_l2. The mechanism is separately falsified if emu_rmse_raw > 5*sigma (=0.005) while refinement still helps (that would mean the gain came from something other than likelihood information), or if emu_rmse_raw <= 5*sigma and the gate still rejects refinement (that would mean the emulator is accurate but the LM objective is non-identifying, pointing at k1/k4 shadowing).
data.if_fails: If the gate rejects refinement with emu_rmse_raw >> sigma, a generic MLP emulator is the bottleneck. A physics-structured emulator (sum of decaying exponentials in time, with rates as functions of log k) would be the next step. If the emulator is accurate yet refinement does not help, then the information content, not the learner, limits accuracy. The CRLB from J^T W J then bounds every arm, and pursuing rel_l2 below it is futile.
data.response_to_critic: (1) Emulator bias in raw units: accepted. The revised code estimates per-channel emulator error on a 15% internal holdout of the training split, in raw units. It weights residuals by 1/(emu_var_raw + sigma^2), so the likelihood is honestly emulator-error-weighted. It also stores emu_rmse_raw for comparison against sigma=0.001. Crucially, it self-gates: refinement is used only if it improves holdout rel_l2 by at least 1% over the inverse net. Your counterexample (structured emulator bias pulling estimates off) therefore degrades to the inverse net rather than below it. This is selection on training data only. (2) Adam replaced by batched Levenberg-Marquardt using a finite-difference emulator Jacobian, box projection in log-k, and per-sample adaptive damping. (3) Emulator ensemble: 2 members, averaged, which reduces variance; the holdout residual gives the calibrated per-channel variance. 3 members was judged too costly for a 400 s portfolio. (4) Runtime: 400 epochs on 85% of the data, three 3-layer width-256 nets, about 30-45 s. This reconciles with the rule estimate better than the earlier 60-110 s. CRLB: the J^T W J matrix computed inside the refinement is exactly the Fisher infor

title: Lemma (Theorem 4.3 in \cite{lyu2019gradient}) — Early Stage Convergence and Global Convergence of Training Mildly Parameterized Neural Networks
text:
The loss decreases at a rate proportional to one over the product of the cumulative learning rate and its logarithm. This holds after an initial time when the loss falls below a threshold. The learning rate must be chosen inversely proportional to the loss and its logarithmic factors. The cumulative learning rate is the sum of learning rates from the initial time to the current step. Under Assumption \ref{def: exponential type loss} on the loss function, let $\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)$ be the parameters of model \eqref{equ: model 2NN nobias} trained by GD \eqref{equ: alg GD}.
If $\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(T_0))<\frac{\tilde{\ell}(0)}{n}$ and the learning rate $\eta_{t}=\mathcal{O}\Big(\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)){\rm poly}\log\frac{1}{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t))}}\Big)$ $(t\geq T_0)$, then we have:

\]

title: Theorem 6 (Local Volatility Bound) — LiveVal: Time-aware Data Valuation via Adaptive Reference Points
text: The volatility of a data point's valuation during training is bounded by a specific expression. This bound depends on the learning rate and the maximum gradient norm. It also inversely depends on the distance to a reference parameter point. The bound holds under conditions of bounded gradients and a minimum distance from the reference. Suppose that for all model parameters $\boldsymbol {\theta }$ and data points $i$, the gradient norms are bounded by $\| \nabla _{\boldsymbol {\theta }} L(f(\mathbf{x}_i; \boldsymbol {\theta }), y_i)\|  \leq G$, and the distance to the reference point satisfies $\| \Delta \boldsymbol {\theta }_t\|  \geq D_{\min } > 0$. Then, for any data point $i$ at training step $t$, the volatility of the step-wise data valuation $v_i^{t}$ is bounded by:\begin{equation}  \sigma _i^{[t]} \leq \frac{2 \eta _t G}{\| \Delta \boldsymbol {\theta }_t\| }, \end{equation}where $\eta _t$ is the learning rate at step $t$.

author: researcher-exploratory
title: TheoremSearch: Fisher information / Cramer-Rao bound for piecewise-constant conductivity from interior point sensor
text: Fisher information / Cramer-Rao bound for piecewise-constant conductivity from interior point sensors in the heat equation The inequality bounds the Fisher information of the heat semigroup applied to a function. It states that the Fisher information of the evolved function is at most the heat semigroup applied to a specific expression. This expression involves the original Fisher information and the squared gradient of the function. The constant and time parameter appear in the bound. The Fisher information between the evolved measures under the heat semigroup is bounded by a constant times a ratio. This ratio involves a chi-squared divergence term, dimension, and a logarithmic factor divided by time. The bound holds when the initial chi-squared divergence is at most one. The Fisher information is expressed as an integral of squared gradient differences of log-densities. Under bounded curvature and derivative conditions, the Fisher information of the heat semigroup applied to a smooth density is bounded by an exponential decay term multiplied by the square of the relative entropy. The bound depends on the lower Ricci curvature bound, the infinity norms of the curvature tensor and its derivatives, and an integral term. In the case of non-positive derivative of N and Ricci curvature bounded below, the bound includes a squared sum of terms. When Ricci curvature is exactly constant and the derivative of N is zero, the bound is similar but with an additional factor of the dimension. A parametric statistical model with an invertible Fisher information metric is considered. A stationary estimator for a cost function at a point is given. Under the condition that the Hessian form at that point is invertible, a generalized Cramer-Rao bound holds. The bound states that the covariance of any cotangent vector is at least the inverse Fisher metric applied to that vector.

author: researcher-ml
title: TheoremSearch: Per-sensor histogram of training readings / sigma, and the fraction of readings <= 0 at each sensor
text: Per-sensor histogram of training readings / sigma, and the fraction of readings <= 0 at each sensor Given input histograms with specified sensitivity bounds, using a particular noise scale and threshold, the algorithm achieves approximate concentrated differential privacy. The privacy guarantee holds with parameters that depend on the input sensitivities and chosen privacy values. The threshold is set using the inverse of the normal cumulative distribution function. This ensures the method meets the stated privacy definition under the given conditions. The noisy count of a histogram cell is at least half of a threshold value with high probability. This holds when the threshold is sufficiently large relative to privacy parameters. The probability of this event is at least 0.75. The threshold depends logarithmically on the inverse of the failure probability and inversely on the privacy parameter. The Stability based Histogram algorithm satisfies epsilon-delta differential privacy. For any domain point with zero true count, the estimated count is exactly zero. For points with a positive true count, the expected absolute error is bounded. The error is at most on the order of one over epsilon times the minimum of the log of one over delta and the true count. If a histogram from a given algorithm has L2-sensitivity 1, then the algorithm is differentially private with parameters epsilon and delta. This holds when noise is drawn from a normal distribution with zero mean and variance sigma squared. The noise scale sigma and threshold rho must satisfy two conditions. The first condition involves cumulative distribution functions and exponential terms bounded by delta over 2, while the second requires rho to exceed a maximum expression involving sigma, delta, and an inverse cumulative distribution function.

Then Algorithm~\ref {alg:meta} is $(\epsilon , \delta )$-$DP$ when the \textsf {Noise} distribution is $\mathcal N (0,\sigma ^2)$ where $\sigma $ and the threshold $\rho $ are chosen s.t. \begin {align*} &\Phi \left (\frac {1}{2\sigma }-\epsilon \sigma \right )-e^\epsilon \Phi \left (-\frac {1}{2\sigma }-\epsilon \sigma \right )\le \frac {\delta }{2} \text { and}\\ &\rho \geq \max _{1\le t \le \Delta _0}\left (1+\sigma \Phi ^{-1}\left (\left (1-\frac {\delta }{2}\right )^{1/t}\right )\right ). \end {align*}
ref.slogan: If a histogram from a given algorithm has L2-sensitivity 1, then the algorithm is differentially private with parameters epsilon and delta. This holds when noise is drawn from a normal distribution with zero mean and variance sigma squared. The noise scale sigma and threshold rho must satisfy two conditions. The first condition involves cumulative distribution functions and exponential terms bounded by delta over 2, while the second requires rho to exceed a maximum expression involving sigma, delta, and an inverse cumulative distribution function.

author: researcher-mathematical
title: Noise-floor PCA in the isotropic (raw-unit) noise metric with box-constrained k-space MMSE loss: whitened deep ensemble
text: The sensor-noise covariance is sigma^2 I in raw temperature units. Two consequences follow. (a) PCA computed on raw centred traces separates signal from noise cleanly: retain the components with eigenvalue > 4 sigma^2. That threshold sits above the Marchenko-Pastur noise edge, about sigma^2 (1 + sqrt(d/n))^2 ≈ 2.3 sigma^2 for d ≈ 800 and n ≈ 3000. Per-feature standardisation, as used in P-011, P-012 and P-013, breaks this isotropy and inflates near-zero-variance channels to unit scale. Examples are early-time readings at the outer sensors (indices 5 and 35), which are almost pure noise. (b) For the rel_l2 metric, the Bayes-optimal estimator is close to the posterior mean of k in k-space, not exp(E[log k]). A head of the form k = 0.5 + 1.5·sigmoid(z), trained with per-sample relative squared error, targets that quantity and respects the uniform box prior exactly. Prediction: this preprocessing plus loss reaches val rel_l2 < 0.05 at full data. It should also beat the matched standard-scaled, log-target MLP cells (P-011/P-013) by at least 10% relative. Per-parameter errors should be ordered k2, k3 < k1, k4, because the pulse at x = 0.5 reaches segments 1 and 4 late and weakly. Mathematically, the inverse map acts on y = F(k) + e with e ~ N(0, sigma^2 I). The local Fisher information is J^T J / sigma^2, where J is the Jacobian of F in raw units. Any information-preserving preconditioning should therefore treat raw-unit directions isotropically. The column space of J over the prior sits in a low-dimensional subspace, which the leading raw-unit PCs capture. The complement carries only noise, so discarding it loses essentially no Fisher information while removing hundreds of pure-noise inputs. With isotropic noise, noise injection can be done exactly in PC coordinates: an orthonormal projection of N(0, sigma^2 I) is N(0, sigma^2 I_r). This makes augmentation cheap and free of the noise_scale ambiguity. The output parametrisation encodes the known support [0.5, 2] and positivity. The training loss matches the evaluation metric, rather than relying on the log-target surrogate, whose exponentiated estimate is biased toward the posterior median or geometric mean. This addresses the open critic disagreement on posterior-mean versus MAP-like estimation, and the noise_scale ambiguity, without a forward model. Training features are already noisy with i.i.d. N(0, 0.001^2) per reading in raw units, as stated in the facts. The harness passes raw features unchanged when features='raw', scaler='none', pca=0. Each target row has 4 entries, k1..k4, in [0.5, 2]. The rel_l2 metric is a per-sample or aggregate relative L2 error on k in original units. Under either definition, per-sample relative MSE is a close surrogate. The signal subspace has dimension much smaller than d; its rank is capped at 64.

data.falsifiable_test: Primary: full-data val rel_l2 < 0.05. Secondary: improvement of at least 10% relative over the best standard-scaled, log-target torch_mlp cell (P-011/P-013) at equal data. Diagnostics: log the retained rank r. The hypothesis predicts 4 <= r << 64, with a visible eigenvalue gap above 4 sigma^2. Per-parameter RMSE should satisfy RMSE(k1), RMSE(k4) > RMSE(k2), RMSE(k3). Falsification conditions: (i) r hits the cap of 64 with no spectral gap, so the low-rank signal assumption fails; (ii) val rel_l2 >= the P-013 anchor; or (iii) per-parameter ordering is reversed.
data.if_fails: If the result matches P-010/P-013 within noise, preprocessing and loss are not the bottleneck. The remaining gap is then either approximation-limited (resolve with a learning curve) or information-limited (resolve with the P-014 CRLB). If r saturates at 64, the signal manifold has non-negligible curvature in many directions, which argues against PCA-based arms such as P-012. If k1/k4 dominate the error, the floor is an identifiability limit set by the pulse location, and only a better estimator of the posterior mean, not more capacity, can help.

author: researcher-ml
title: abandoned: Factorial cell: torch_mlp on log features with log-k targets (contrast against raw-feature arms)
text: Negative/null result. At pilot fidelity (300 train, 60 val), log features (0.0542) are indistinguishable from raw features (0.0526-0.0587, seed spread ~0.006). The predicted degradation from near-zero log-feature noise did not materialise beyond noise. The proposal's own counter-mechanism (late-time log-linear decay) was shown to be inapplicable because of the CFL-bounded window. A full-fidelity run would cost ~40 s for a contrast expected to fall within seed spread, which is poor value under the budget. Recorded conclusion: the feature transform (raw vs log) is not the accuracy-limiting factor for the MLP. The team should not spend budget tuning feature transforms, and should keep 'raw' as the default for the KRR/MLP arms. Caveat: if a later zero-cost SNR diagnostic shows more than 10% of sensor-5/35 readings below 5*sigma AND a full-fidelity arm reports per-parameter errors dominated by k1/k4, this contrast could be revisited.

author: researcher-ml
title: Architecture-matched deep ensemble MLP with exact raw-unit sigma=0.001 noise augmentation and k-space averaging
text: With architecture held equal to P-013 ([512,256,128], LayerNorm, GELU, log-k targets), two changes reduce val rel_l2 below 0.05 at full data: (a) fresh raw-unit N(0, 0.001^2) input noise at every minibatch and (b) arithmetic k-space averaging of 3 independently initialised members. Mechanism: (a) acts as a likelihood-matched regulariser that stops the net from memorising the single noise realisation per training sample; (b) removes the initialisation-variance component of the error, which the pilot seed spread (0.0526 vs 0.0587) suggests is ~0.003-0.006. The pilot MLPs sit at 0.053-0.059, just above the 0.05 target, and their seed-to-seed spread is of the same order as the gap to the target. That is the regime where variance reduction is most likely to matter. Explicit raw-unit noise removes the factor-1000 noise_scale ambiguity between P-011 and P-013 by construction. Arithmetic averaging in k space matches the evaluation metric, since rel_l2 on k is minimised by the posterior mean of k, not of log k. custom_ml receives unscaled raw sensor readings when scaler='none' and pca=0, so the per-channel noise std in input units is exactly 0.001 y is an (n, 4) array of conductivities in [0.5, 2] Effective training noise is sqrt(2)*sigma (the existing realisation plus the injected one). title: Augmentation-off control for the P-013 anchor: torch_mlp raw/log-k with noise_aug=0
text: At sigma=0.001 the sensor noise is small relative to trace variation over the prior box, except possibly at early times on end sensors. The anchor MLP's error is therefore dominated by approximation and information structure, not noise overfitting. Prediction: noise_aug=0 lands within ±10% relative val rel_l2 of the P-013 aug2 (multiplier=1) cell. The competing explanation is that noise regularisation matters, in which case aug0 is more than 10% worse. That would imply the network exploits sub-sigma fine structure, which is consistent with an ill-conditioned map in some directions, likely k1/k4. This is the single missing control named by the critic and by my original proposal. It isolates the augmentation factor in the shared factorial, and it arbitrates the noise_scale semantics question without reading harness source. It complements P-010, which injects explicit raw-unit noise: if P-010 ≈ P-013-aug2 ≠ aug0, the multiplier reading is confirmed. P-013 uses the architecture and optimiser settings below. If not, the harness should copy P-013's exact params and change only noise_aug. noise_scale is a multiplier on sigma (pilot-supported). It is irrelevant here because noise_aug=0. Train, val and test share the simulator and noise model. Single-seed differences under about 10% relative are not interpretable (pilot spread 0.053-0.059).

author: researcher-experimental
title: Preprocessing contrast for kernel ridge: unscaled PCA vs standardised PCA (P-006) on the same KRR cell
text: Standardisation before PCA inflates noise-dominated, near-constant channels (early-time and boundary-sensor readings) to unit variance. PCA components are then wasted on noise, which degrades the isotropic RBF. With scaler='none', the 30 leading PCs capture the parabolic signal modes. Prediction: at full data, the unscaled KRR beats the standardised KRR cell (P-006 config) by at least 10% relative val rel_l2. Competing explanation: if the discriminative information for k1/k4 lives in low-amplitude channels, removing standardisation discards it, and unscaled will be worse. Data-distribution view. Heat traces are dominated by a few decaying modes, but amplitudes differ by orders of magnitude across sensors and times. The scaling choice decides whether PCA truncation acts as denoising or as information loss. This is the cheapest arm (seconds), and it directly tests the claimed approximately 4-D manifold structure that underpins all compressed-feature approaches. scaler='none' skips standardisation, and PCA is applied to centred raw features. Whitening after PCA is unknown. If absent, the RBF sees variance-weighted PCs. The gamma heuristic (gamma_mult / (n_features·Var(X))) adapts to the unscaled overall variance, so gamma_mult=1 remains in a sensible range. The P-006 standardised config is run at full data as the comparison. If only the 10%-data pilot exists, the contrast must be rerun at matched data size.

Secondary checks: the PCA explained-variance spectrum (unscaled vs standardised), and pca=10 vs 60 if budget allows. Error flat across pca values implies a low-dimensional manifold.
data.if_fails: If unscaled is worse, the discriminative signal is in low-variance channels. Feature design should then emphasise per-sensor/per-time normalisation (log features, P-009) or learned features rather than PCA truncation. If both KRR variants stay above 0.06 while the MLP is below 0.05, an isotropic kernel is inadequate and the map is anisotropic.

title: Learned-emulator information arbiter: Jacobian CRLB for rel_l2, plus empirically gated emulator-LM refinement of a sigma-augmented amortized inverse
text: (H1, primary) An MLP emulator log k -> traces trained on about 2550 pairs reaches holdout error well below the channel std (emu_rel_std < 2%). Its Jacobian-based CRLB for per-sample rel_l2 at sigma=0.001 is below 0.03. If so, the 0.053-0.059 pilot errors are approximation-limited, not information-limited, and learners can cross 0.05. (H2, secondary) Refinement toward the amortized estimate under the emulator likelihood lowers internal-holdout rel_l2 by at least 3% relative to the sigma-augmented inverse net. If not, the gate disables it and the method equals its inverse net. The team's central disagreement (approximation vs information floor) has no arbiter without a forward model. The data pairs define an empirical forward map. Its Jacobian gives a Fisher information and hence a quantitative floor. This is a cross-tradition move: estimation theory plus variational data assimilation through a learned surrogate. It is structurally distinct from the 5 purely amortized data-driven arms. The emulator Jacobian approximates the true sensitivity well enough at the holdout points. This is checked indirectly through emu_rel_std. Features are flattened sensor time series, ordering is irrelevant, bounds are [0.5, 2] and sigma=0.001, all hard-coded per the problem statement. rel_l2 is the per-sample mean of ||e||/||k||. The CRLB is computed for that definition by the delta method. The CRLB bounds unbiased estimators only. The prior can beat it on weakly identified segments.

In that case the information floor (unbiased-estimator sense) is binding and further learner tuning is futile, except via prior exploitation. H2 is falsified if the gate rejects refinement (hold_rel[1] >= 0.97*hold_rel[0]), or if val rel_l2 is not at least 3% below the inverse-net-only value (refine_iters=0 run, same seed). The gate threshold is fixed at 0.97 before the run.
data.if_fails: If crlb_rel is small but learners stall near 0.05, the gap is approximation or optimisation, so invest in data efficiency (ensembles, physics-structured features). If crlb_param for k1/k4 is large, the error is information-limited on the outer segments. Then the posterior mean, which shrinks toward 1.25, is the right estimator and no refinement can help. If the emulator itself is poor (emu_rel_std >= 2%), a physics-structured emulator (sum of decaying modes, with rates in log k) is the next step.
data.response_to_critic: (1) Posterior mean vs MAP. Accepted in substance. LM toward a MAP point can only help if the amortized net is far from Bayes. The revision makes three changes. First, the inverse initializer is now noise-augmented with exact raw-unit sigma, so it is a posterior-mean approximant comparable to P-010/P-013. Second, the LM prior term pulls toward this amortized estimate (prior_w*||z - z_init||^2) rather than toward the box centre. On flat-likelihood directions such as k1/k4, the solution therefore stays at the posterior-mean-like value instead of wandering along the ridge, which addresses the counterexample directly. Third, refinement is self-gated EMPIRICALLY: it is enabled only if it lowers the internal-holdout rel_l2 by at least 3%. Since this is the metric itself, the gate cannot be fooled by an emulator-RMSE threshold. (2) The 5*sigma gate is meaningless without signal scale. Accepted. That gate is removed. The code now records emu_rmse_raw, emu_rmse/sigma and emu_rmse/channel-std (emu_rel_std) as diagnostics only. (3) Budget. Accepted. author: scheduler
title: inconclusive: Noise-floor PCA in the isotropic (raw-unit) noise metric with box-constrained k-space MMSE loss: whitened deep ensemble
text: The sensor-noise covariance is sigma^2 I in raw temperature units. Two consequences follow. (a) PCA computed on raw centred traces separates signal from noise cleanly: retain the components with eigenvalue > 4 sigma^2. That threshold sits above the Marchenko-Pastur noise edge, about sigma^2 (1 + sqrt(d/n))^2 ≈ 2.3 sigma^2 for d ≈ 800 and n ≈ 3000. Per-feature standardisation, as used in P-011, P-012 and P-013, breaks this isotropy and inflates near-zero-variance channels to unit scale. Examples are early-time readings at the outer sensors (indices 5 and 35), which are almost pure noise. (b) For the rel_l2 metric, the Bayes-optimal estimator is close to the posterior mean of k in k-space, not exp(E[log k]). A head of the form k = 0.5 + 1.5·sigmoid(z), trained with per-sample relative squared error, targets that quantity and respects the uniform box prior exactly. Prediction: this preprocessing plus loss reaches val rel_l2 < 0.05 at full data. It should also beat the matched standard-scaled, log-target MLP cells (P-011/P-013) by at least 10% relative. Per-parameter errors should be ordered k2, k3 < k1, k4, because the pulse at x = 0.5 reaches segments 1 and 4 late and weakly. prediction {"metric": "rel_l2", "op": "<", "value": 0.05}: method did not produce a full-fidelity validation result
